label: DUI Arrest Without Probable Cause
motion_heading: The Arrest Was Not Supported by Probable Cause

review_conditions.display_note: The officer observed signs the prosecution will rely on (such as odor, speech, balance, or an admission to drinking). Address each one in the argument, including any innocent explanation and anything on video that contradicts it.

Some of what the officer observed cuts against impairment (such as lucid speech, steady balance, or handling documents without difficulty). Make sure those facts are in the record, from the video or the officer's own report, and use them in the argument.

The officer says your client failed at least one field sobriety test, but something may have affected the tests (surface, weather, footwear, a physical condition, instructions, or procedure). Get the video and the officer's training records, and argue the results deserve little weight.

sentences.text: A warrantless arrest is lawful only if the officer has probable cause to believe that the person arrested has committed a crime.

Probable cause exists only where the facts and circumstances within the officer's knowledge, based on reasonably trustworthy information, are sufficient to warrant a prudent person in believing that the person arrested had committed an offense.

While “the odor of alcohol [Officer] Byrnes detected indicated that Saucier had consumed some amount of alcohol . . . the law prohibits driving while intoxicated, not driving after having had a drink.”

_author_notes: REVIEW CAREFULLY (provisional rule, legal judgment not yet reviewed): this issue is suggested on a DUI arrest when the officer observed none of the bad-driving options and the field sobriety tests don't add up to failure (no tests given, none failed, or something affected them). Field sobriety tests are no longer an encounter event (2026-10-12): q_dui_fsts_given is asked for every DUI arrest, blank if none. Observations after the stop don't affect whether it's suggested yet; they drive memo notes. Drafted by Claude on 2026-10-12 as a placeholder until the maintainer supplies Alaska cases with the factors that mattered, which should replace this rule (and print case paragraphs keyed to matching factors).

Supreme Court citations in this file were added from memory (not checked against the opinions) under the maintainer's 'certain SCOTUS cites only' policy: Devenpeck v. Alford, Beck v. Ohio. Unverified; pincites empty.
The three review notes (dui_signs_observed, dui_helpful_facts, dui_fst_problems) are Claude's drafts. applicable_courts is ['scotus'] for now; Alaska-only paragraphs will get ['ak'].
